title: std::shared_ptr, std::weak_ptr and Shared Ownership
objectives: Explain the control block: strong and weak counts, atomic updates, and what happens when each counter reaches zero
Predict use_count() transitions and destructor timing in shared_ptr programs
Choose make_shared over shared_ptr(new) and state its one trade-off with weak_ptr observers
Detect ownership cycles that leak, and break them with std::weak_ptr::lock
motivation: Some objects genuinely have several owners with independent lifetimes: a pricing cache referenced by every strategy, a curve shared by many pricers. std::shared_ptr implements 'last one out turns off the lights' via an atomic reference count in a control block - and std::weak_ptr observes without keeping anything alive, which is also the only cure for shared-ownership cycles. This lesson is about the machinery: refcounts, allocation costs, cycles, and lock().

blocks.text: Shared ownership and the control block

blocks.md: A `std::shared_ptr<T>` is two pointers: one to the **object**, one to a **control block** shared by all smart pointers watching the same object. The control block holds a **strong count** (owners: shared_ptrs keeping the object alive) and a **weak count** (observers: weak_ptrs, plus the strong owners themselves). Copying a shared_ptr increments the strong count *atomically*; destroying one decrements it. When the strong count reaches zero, the object is destroyed; the control block itself survives until the weak count also reaches zero. This is why shared_ptr costs real memory (two words per pointer, plus the block) and real time (atomic read-modify-write on every copy and destruction) - unlike unique_ptr's zero overhead.

rows: strong -1; at 0 the object is destroyed
object destroyed; block lives while weak > 0

blocks.md: `std::shared_ptr<T> p(new T)` performs **two allocations**: the object, then the control block. `std::make_shared<T>(args...)` performs **one**, placing object and block together - faster, and friendlier to the cache since the two live adjacently. The trade-off: with make_shared, the object's storage is inside the same allocation as the block, so while any weak_ptr observer still exists, the *object's memory* cannot be freed even though the object is destroyed (the strong count hit zero - destructor ran - but the block waits for the weak count). For large objects with long-lived weak observers, the two-allocation form can release object memory earlier.

blocks.caption: use_count() reads the strong count; the destructor fires exactly when it reaches zero.

blocks.md: `std::weak_ptr<T>` points into the same control block but never increments the strong count - it only marks the block as watched. It cannot dereference directly: to *use* the object you must call **lock()**, which atomically returns a shared_ptr that either owns the object (if still alive) or is null (if it died). The lock-then-test pattern is the safe one; testing `expired()` first is a race, because the last owner may die between your check and your use. Typical uses: caches that must not pin objects, back-pointers in parent/child graphs, and any observer that should not extend an object's lifetime.

blocks.caption: weak_ptr never keeps the object alive; lock() turns observation into ownership only while it is safe.

blocks.text: The cycle problem - and its cure

blocks.md: Shared ownership has one structural failure mode: **cycles**. If A holds a shared_ptr to B and B holds a shared_ptr to A, each object's strong count is pinned at 1 by the other forever - both leak, and no destructor ever runs. The rule: ownership flows one way (usually parent owns children via shared_ptr); anything pointing *back* must be a weak_ptr.

blocks.caption: Both nodes die because the back edge does not own. With shared_ptr prev instead, both counts stay >= 1 and nothing is ever destroyed.

blocks.title: Cycles in a pricing tree
blocks.md: A scenario tree holds children via shared_ptr; each child needs its parent for calibration lookups. A shared_ptr back-edge leaks the entire tree on every re-calibration. The fix is exactly the weak_ptr back-edge above - a one-word change that determines whether the pricing service's memory grows forever or stays flat.

blocks.title: shared_ptr is not a thread-safety switch
blocks.md: Only the control block is thread-safe (atomic counts). The *managed object* is as thread-safe as any other object: concurrent access still needs mutexes or atomics. Two threads may safely copy different shared_ptr instances to the same object - that is all the guarantee buys.

blocks.caption: Every shared_ptr is two words; the control block is the single source of truth for lifetime.

guidedExercise.prompt:
Track the strong count and object lifetime step by step, and give the value printed at each marked point:

```cpp
auto a = std::make_shared<int>(5);   // (1) strong = ?
auto b = a;                          // (2) strong = ?
{
    auto c = a;                      // (3) strong = ?
    std::cout << a.use_count();      // (4) prints ?
}
b.reset();                           // (5) strong = ?, object destroyed?
// (6) a.use_count() is now ?  and the object is ?
```
hints: Count only strong owners: copies of shared_ptr, not weak_ptrs.
c's scope ends at the closing brace - what does its destructor do to the count?
The object dies exactly when the strong count transitions to zero.
guidedExercise.solution: (1) strong = 1 (the object and control block are created). (2) strong = 2 (copy increments atomically). (3) strong = 3. (4) prints **3**. (5) c was destroyed at the end of its scope (back to 2), then b.reset() takes it to **1** - the object is *not* destroyed, a still owns it. (6) a.use_count() is **1**, and the object is **alive**; it dies only when a is reset or goes out of scope. The invariant to internalise: the destructor fires on the transition to zero, never before.

independentExercise.prompt:
Design a two-way parent/child relationship: class Parent holds a shared_ptr<Child>; class Child needs a reference back to its Parent.

(a) First write it with `std::shared_ptr<Parent> parent_` in the Child. State the exact strong counts after `p->child = c; c->parent = p;` and what happens when p and c go out of scope. (b) Then fix it with `std::weak_ptr<Parent> parent_` and show how Child accesses the parent safely. (c) Report the use_count() values in the fixed version and prove the destructors run.
hints: (a) After both assignments, each object is owned by one stack variable and one object member - what are the counts, and can they ever reach zero?
(b) The child cannot just dereference the weak_ptr - what method converts observation into ownership safely?
(c) In the fixed version the back edge contributes nothing to the strong count.

commonMistakes: Reaching for shared_ptr by default - every copy and destruction is an atomic operation, and shared ownership loosens the design; unique_ptr is the default, shared_ptr is the exception.
Creating cycles with shared_ptr back-pointers: parent owns children, children must weak_ptr back to the parent.
Assuming shared_ptr makes the managed object thread-safe - only the control block counts are atomic; the object itself needs its own synchronisation.
Testing expired() then lock() as two separate calls - the last owner can die in between; call lock() once and test the returned shared_ptr.
Forgetting the make_shared trade-off: object memory stays allocated while any weak observer exists, even though the object is destroyed.
realWorldApplication: Caches, plugin registries and shared configuration objects are the standard use cases: many consumers, independent lifetimes, no single owner - shared_ptr for the cache entries, weak_ptr for observers that must not pin them.
quantFinanceApplication: A yield-curve object shared by every book's pricer is a shared_ptr held in a registry; per-strategy calculations observe it through weak_ptr so a strategy shutting down never pins the curve, and curve re-calibration never leaves a dangling pricer.
summary: shared_ptr = object pointer + control block (atomic strong count, weak count); the object is destroyed when the strong count reaches zero.
make_shared performs one allocation (object + block together) instead of two; trade-off: block lifetime pins object memory while weak observers exist.
weak_ptr observes without owning: it cannot dereference directly; lock() atomically returns a shared_ptr or null, and lock-then-test beats expired()-then-lock.
Shared-ownership cycles leak permanently; the cure is direction of ownership - owning edges one way, weak_ptr for back-edges.
Thread-safety applies only to the control block; the shared object still needs its own synchronisation.

quiz.explanation: a creates the object (strong 1); b copies it (2); reset takes b to null (1); a.reset() drops the strong count to 0, which destroys the object ('dtor'), then 'done' prints.

weak_ptr assignment does not change the strong count, so use_count() prints 1. lock() returns a valid shared_ptr, dereferencing prints 42. After the scope, the strong count hit zero: expired() is true and lock() returns null, so 'failed' prints.

quiz.prompt: After running `auto s = std::make_shared<int>(1); auto a = s; auto b = s; a.reset(); b.reset();` - what is s.use_count()?
quiz.explanation: Three owners (strong 3), then a.reset() and b.reset() each decrement: 3 -> 2 -> 1. Only s still owns the object, which is therefore still alive.

quiz.prompt: In the shared_ptr control-block model, when exactly is the *control block* itself freed?
options: When the strong count reaches zero
When the weak count reaches zero (and strong is already zero)
When the last shared_ptr goes out of scope, regardless of weak_ptr observers
It is never freed; the block is reused by the allocator
quiz.explanation: Strong count zero destroys the object; the block must outlive weak_ptr observers (they read it in lock()), so it is freed when the weak count also reaches zero. This is why make_shared object memory persists while weak observers exist.

quiz.prompt: Two objects hold std::shared_ptr to each other and both stack pointers are destroyed. What happens?
options: Nothing: each object's strong count stays at 1, pinned by the other - both leak and no destructor runs
The compiler detects the cycle and deletes the older object
One object is destroyed and the other dangles
quiz.explanation: Each object owns the other, so neither strong count can reach zero: a permanent leak. The fix is to make one direction (typically the back-pointer) a weak_ptr.

quiz.prompt: Why is the pattern `if (!w.expired()) { auto p = w.lock(); use(*p); }` unsafe, and what is the correct pattern?
quiz.modelAnswer: The last strong owner may destroy the object between the expired() check and the lock() call, so lock() can still return null and the use is invalid. Correct: call lock() once - `if (auto p = w.lock()) { use(*p); }` - since lock() atomically converts observation into ownership.
quiz.explanation: expired()-then-lock() is a check-then-act race on another thread's destruction. lock() performs the check and the acquisition atomically, returning either a owning shared_ptr or null - a single decision point.

flashcards.front: What does the shared_ptr control block contain?
flashcards.back: An atomic strong count (owning shared_ptrs), a weak count (weak_ptrs), and the deleter/allocator. Object destroyed at strong == 0; block freed at weak == 0.
make_shared: one allocation, object adjacent to block - faster and cache-friendlier. Trade-off: object memory persists until the weak count drops, even after the destructor runs.
A shared_ptr that owns the object if it is still alive, or a null shared_ptr if it is not - the check and acquisition are one atomic operation.

flashcards.front: Parent holds shared_ptr<Child>; Child holds shared_ptr<Parent>. Bug?
flashcards.back: Ownership cycle: both strong counts pinned at 1 forever, both leak. Fix: Child holds weak_ptr<Parent> and uses lock().

flashcards.front: Is the shared object thread-safe because shared_ptr is?
flashcards.back: No - only the control block counts are atomic. Concurrent access to the managed object needs its own mutex/atomics.
